searchDoc.body: MemPalace is a local-first AI memory system: it stores every word you share verbatim, indexes it as a spatial memory palace of wings, rooms, and drawers, and retrieves it with hybrid semantic plus keyword search, all on your own machine with no API key required for the core path. It never summarizes, never paraphrases, and never phones home. The name comes from the ancient method of loci combined with Niklas Luhmann's Zettelkasten: wings group broad categories (people, projects, topics), rooms group by day or session, and drawers hold immutable verbatim chunks of about 800 characters. A separate index layer called closets stores compact AAAK pointer lines (entities, topics, key quotes) that an LLM can scan in one pass to know exactly which drawer to open. This wiki is a deep, cross-linked map written for both humans browsing the architecture and agents grepping for the exact module, symbol, and line. The core idea is to separate storage from retrieval: content is stored structured and lossless, but found unstructured. The AAAK index is a ranking signal, never a gate, so a weak or missing pointer can only help a search, never hide a drawer, which is why 100 percent recall is the design requirement rather than a side effect. Retrieval is hybrid vector plus BM25, reaching about 96.6 percent recall at 5 with zero LLM on LongMemEval, 98.4 percent held-out through the full hybrid pipeline, and at or above 99 percent with optional model-agnostic reranking. The codebase is roughly 30,000 lines of Python across about 48 modules at version 3.3.6, exposing 29 Model-Context-Protocol tools so agents can live inside the palace, with 14 UI locales and over 100 embedding languages. Seven design principles are non-negotiable: verbatim always, incremental only, entity-first, local-first with zero external API by default, performance budgets (hooks under 500 ms, injection under 100 ms), privacy by architecture, and background everything. Background hooks file memory off the chat window, saving roughly one US dollar per session by never re-transmitting diary blocks. Explore the major areas from here: ingestion (project mining, conversation mining, entities, AAAK dialect), retrieval (search, knowledge graph, storage backends), interfaces (CLI, MCP server, hooks), and the cross-cutting concerns of LLM integration, internationalization, security and privacy, maintenance, and benchmarks. Every page links to its neighbors, and the knowledge-graph diagram shows how the areas connect.
